title: Chapter 62 — The Dart
paragraphs: A word concerning an incident in the last chapter.

According to the unvarying custom of the fishery, the whale-boat pushes off from the ship with the headsman or whale-killer as temporary steersman, and the harpooner pulling the foremost oar, known as the harpooner-oar. Now it takes a strong, steady arm to throw the first iron into the fish. For often, in what is called a long dart, the heavy iron weapon has to be flung fifty feet or more. And no matter how powerful the arm, this distance puts real strain on it. So the harpooner needs all the rest he can get. But the very act that should give him that rest — rowing — instead drains him of the very energy he needs most. For to pull in a whale-boat is not a child's game. Often the harpooner must pull hard for several exhausting hours on end. Now, where is the point of tiring out the one man you need most? In the harpooner's oar he must pull harder than any other man in the boat. And if pulling does not fatigue his arms, the fixed, concentrated attention required to keep the oar precisely in its place surely must — since in a whale chase, oars are wielded with utmost precision. Furthermore, if the harpooner reaches his target too exhausted for a good throw, he is given barely a second to recover before the line runs. Then what happens? In practice, the line seizes him with all the strength of gravity multiplied by speed.

Again, if the dart is successful — that is, when the whale starts to run — the boathead and harpooner must likewise start running from one end of the boat to the other, to the serious danger of themselves and everyone else. It is then they swap places, and the headsman, the chief officer of the little craft, takes his proper station in the bow.

Now, I do not care who says otherwise — all this is both foolish and unnecessary. The headsman should stay in the bow from first to last. He should both throw the harpoon and wield the lance, and no rowing whatsoever should be expected of him, except under circumstances obvious to any fisherman. I know this would sometimes mean a slight loss of speed in the chase, but the long experience of the entire fishery would confirm this is far more than compensated for by the greater accuracy of the throw.
To ensure the greatest power in the dart, the harpooners of this world must spring to their feet from rest, not from exhaustion.
